אב.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔabw-. Doublet of אַבָּא (ába), which was borrowed from Aramaic. Cognate with Arabic أب.

אבד.etymologyText: Compare Moabite אבד ('-b-d, “to perish”), Aramaic אֲבַד ('avad), Classical Syriac [script needed] ('evad, “he perished”), Ugaritic [script needed] ('bd, “to perish”)

אבה.etymologyText: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔabay-. Compare Akkadian 𒁍𒀪𒄿𒌈 (bu-ʾ-i-tum /⁠buʾītu⁠/, “a thing wished, willed, desired”), Arabic أَبَى (ʔabā, “he rejected, refused, was unwilling, unwilling to do otherwise; originally to hold back, to desire to stay or wish to remain”) and the root ء ب ب (ʔ b b, “to prepare to go out for”) in the phrase أَبَّ إِلَى (ʔabba ʔilā, “to long after, to want to go forth to, to yearn or have a desire to go to something”), Egyptian ꜣbj (“to desire, to want, to be h

אגוז.etymologyText: Borrowed from Aramaic גּוֹזָא (gōzā), אמגוזא, from unattested Old Persian *angauza, see Old Armenian ընկոյզ (ənkoyz) for more.

אגם.etymologyText: Borrowed into West Semitic from Akkadian 𒀀𒂵𒈬𒌝 (agammum), from Sumerian 𒀀𒂵𒄠 (agam). Compare Classical Syriac ܐܓܡܐ (ʾaḡmā, “marsh, swamp”) and Arabic أَجَمَة (ʔajama, “jungle, brushwood”).

אדון.etymologyText: Perhaps related to דִּין (dín, “law”) or from Proto-Semitic *ʾadan- (“to rule, judge”). Compare Ugaritic 𐎀𐎄𐎚 (ảdt, “lady”), Phoenician 𐤀𐤃𐤍 (ʾdn, “lord”), Ancient Greek Ἄδωνις (Ádōnis, “mortal lover of the goddess Aphrodite”).

אדם.etymologyText: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔadam-. Comparable to Phoenician 𐤀𐤃𐤌 (ʾdm, “man, earthling”), Ugaritic 𐎀𐎄𐎎 (ảdm, “man; red earth, red ochre”), Old South Arabian 𐩱𐩵𐩣 (ʾdm, “vassals, subjects”), Ge'ez ዶም (dom, “slave”), Akkadian 𒀀𒁕𒄠𒈬 (a-da-am-mu /⁠adamu⁠/, “blood”), Akkadian 𒀀𒁕𒈠𒌈 (a-da-ma-tum /⁠adamātu⁠/, “dark red earth or dye”), Akkadian 𒀀𒁕𒈬 (a-da-mu /⁠adamu⁠/, “a red garment”), Akkadian 𒀀𒁕𒈬 (a-da-mu /⁠adamu⁠/, “an important or noble person”).

אדרמלך.etymologyText: Derived from Akkadian 𒀭𒁇𒂷𒆪 (A-dar-milku) or 𒀭𒊩𒌆𒅁𒂷𒆪 (A-dar-ra-milku).

או.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔaw. Cognate with Arabic أَوْ (ʔaw) and Ugaritic 𐎜 (ʾō).

אריה.etymologyText: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔarway-. Cognate with Ge'ez አርዌ (ʾärwe, “animal, beast”). By surface analysis, אֲרִי +‎ ־ֵה.

אז.etymologyText: Cognate to Aramaic אֱדַיִן (ʾĕḏáyin, “then, at that time”), Arabic إِذ (ʔiḏ), إِذَا (ʔiḏā), إِذًا (ʔiḏan).

אזוב.etymologyText: Related to Classical Syriac ܙܘܦܐ (zōṗā), Akkadian 𒍪𒌑𒁍 (/⁠zūpu⁠/), Jewish Palestinian Aramaic אֵיזוֹבָא (ʾēzōḇa), Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos).

אחות.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔaḫwat-. Cognate with Arabic أخت.

אחמתא.etymologyText: Borrowed from Aramaic אַחְמְתָא (ʾaḥməṯā), eventually from Old Persian 𐏃𐎥𐎶𐎫𐎠𐎴 (h-g-m-t-a-n /⁠Haⁿgmatānaʰ⁠/). Doublet of Doublet of המדאן. Cognate with English Ecbatana, English Hamadan, and Persian همدان (hamedân).

אטר.etymologyText: Biblical hapax legomenon, cognate with Arabic أَطَرَ (to bend, curve).

אי.etymologyText: Compare Egyptian jw (“island”) and Phoenician 𐤀𐤉 (ʾy). Probably related to Arabic أوى (“to look for shelter; to retreat”) and cognate to an Arabic form *أِوْي (*ʔiwy).

איב.etymologyText: Possibly cognate with Arabic وَئِبَ (waʔiba, “to get angry (with)”).

איוב.etymologyText: Possibly from early northwest Semitic dialectal name meaning "where is the father?" from אַי (ʾay, “where”) and אוֹבּ (ʾôb, “father”), dialectal variant of אב ('áv, “father”). Or, akin to אויב (oyév, “enemy”).[1] Some biblical scholars have suggested that it is related to Arabic أَوَّاب (ʔawwāb, “returning”), from the root ء و ب (ʔ w b).

אין.etymologyText: Compare Ugaritic 𐎛𐎐 (ỉn) and Arabic إِنْ (ʔin).

אכל.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔakal-. Compare Aramaic אֲכַל (ʾăḵal), Arabic أَكَلَ (ʔakala).

אל.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʾil-. Cognate with Akkadian 𒀭 (ilum), Arabic إِل (ʔil), إِلَٰه (ʔilāh), Aramaic אלה (aláh).

אלא.etymologyText: Related to Arabic إِلَّا (ʔillā), Ge'ez አላ (ʾälla).

אלדעה.etymologyText: From אֵל (el, “god, deity”) +‎ דָּעָה (da'a, “to call”). Note that דעה is an unused construction coming from the root י־ד־ע (y-d-') relating to "knowing". A similar construction is found in the Arabic دَعَا (da'a, “to call”). The name thus can be translated as "the one whom God calls".

אלמנה.etymologyText: Possibly from the root א־ל־ם, and if so comparable to Arabic أَلَم (ʔalam, “pain, ache”). But compare also Aramaic אַרְמַלְתָּא (ʾarmaltā) and Arabic أَرْمَلَة (ʔarmala). One of the two consonantisms is likely due to assimilation and dissimilation processes.

אלף.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔalp- (“thousand; cattle”). Cognate with Arabic ألف (ʔalf).

אנוש.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔināš-. Max Wagner thinks it is an old borrowing from Aramaic אֱינָשׁ (ʾěnāš) under Hebraization of the vocalism.

אנחנו.etymologyText: From Biblical Hebrew 𐤀𐤍𐤇𐤍𐤅 (ʾnḥnw), from Proto-Semitic *niḥnu. Cognate with Arabic نَحْنُ (naḥnu).

אסתר.etymologyText: Said to be borrowed from Old Persian [script needed] (sitareh, “star”), from Proto-Iranian *Hstā́ (“star”), or Akkadian Ištar (“Ishtar”).[1]

אפעה.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔapʕaw-, compare Arabic أَفْعًى (ʔafʕan), Eblaite 𒉌𒁀𒅇𒌝 (ì-pá-ù-um), and Ugaritic 𐎀𐎔𐎓 (ảpʿ).

אצר.etymologyText: Cognate with Aramaic אֲצַר and Arabic أَصَرَ (ʔaṣara, “to confine, to shut up, to restrain”).

שטר.etymologyText: From Akkadian 𒊬 (šaṭārum, “written document”). Also borrowed into Arabic سَطْر (saṭr).

שלג.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ṯalg- (“snow”). Cognate with Akkadian 𒊭𒀠𒄖𒌝 (šalgum) and Arabic ثَلْج (ṯalj).

שלום.etymologyText: Etymologically related to שָׁלָה (šālâ, “to be quiet, tranquil”). Compare also שָׁלַו (šālaw, “to be quiet, at ease”). Common Northwest Semitic, Phoenician 𐤔𐤋𐤌 (šlm /⁠šalōm⁠/), Aramaic שְׁלָמָא (šlāmā) / ܫܠܡܐ (šlāmā), Ugaritic 𐎌𐎍𐎎 (šlm /⁠šalāmu⁠/). Cognate with Arabic سلام (salām).

שלט.etymologyText: Cognate with Arabic سَلَّطَ (sallaṭa), Classical Syriac ܫܰܠܚܬ.

שלמנאסר.etymologyText: From Akkadian Salmānu-ašarēd (“Shulmanu is foremost”). Cognate with Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܫܠܡܢܥܣܪ (šalmāniˁsar) and Classical Syriac ܫܠܡܢܥܣܪ (šalmanaʿsar).

שם.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *šim-, from Proto-Afroasiatic *sim- (“name”). Cognate with Arabic اسم (ism, “name”) and Aramaic שְׁמָא (šəmā).

שמאל.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *śimaʔl-. Cognate with Arabic شِمَال (šimāl), Akkadian 𒆏 (šumēlum), Aramaic סְמָלָא (səmālā), שְׂמָאלָא (śəmālā), ܣܸܡܵܠܵܐ (semmālā), Ugaritic 𐎌𐎎𐎀𐎍 (šmảl). The north sense derives from the direction being on the left side facing the sunrise, this sense also exists in Arabic.

שמיכה.etymologyText: Perhaps from an unused verb in the root ס־מ־ך (s-m-k), alternatively borrowed from Aramaic מַשְׁכָּא.

שמע.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *šamiʕ-. Cognate with Arabic سَمِعَ (samiʕa, “to hear”).

שנן.etymologyText: Cognate with Aramaic שְׁנַן (shnan, “to sharpen”) and Arabic سَنَّ (sanna, “to sharpen”).

שנער.etymologyText: Related to Akkadian 𒆠𒂗𒄀 (Šumerum, “Sumer”), Egyptian sꜣngꜣr (“Babylonia”), Hittite 𒋗𒈨𒊒 (/⁠šanhar(a)⁠/), all likely ultimately from Sumerian 𒌦𒊕𒈪𒂵 (ug̃₃ sag̃-gig₂-ga /⁠ug̃ Sag̃-Giga⁠/, “Sumerians”, literally “black-headed people”) or 𒆠𒂗𒄀 (ki-en-gi /⁠Kengir⁠/, “Sumer”, literally “place of the noble lords”).

שעה.etymologyText: From Aramaic שעתא (šāʿəṯā). Cognate with Arabic سَاعَة (sāʕa).

שפך.etymologyText: Cognate to Arabic سَفَك (safak, “to shed, spill”).

שקל.etymologyText: From the root שׁ־ק־ל (sh-q-l), in the pa`ál conjugation. From Proto-Semitic *ṯql (“to weigh; burden, weight”); cognate with Arabic ثقل and Aramaic תקל.

שרה.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *śarār (“to rule”). Cognate with Akkadian 𒊩𒈗 (šarratum, “queen”).

שתל.etymologyText: Already in Canaanite times loaned from Akkadian [script needed] (satālu).

תאנה.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *tiʔin-. Cognate to Arabic تين (tīn).

תבן.etymologyText: Cognate with Aramaic תִּבְנָא / ܬܒܢܐ (teḇnā, “straw”) whence Arabic تِبْن (tibn) and cognate to or derived from Akkadian 𒅔𒉡𒁕 (/⁠tibnu⁠/, “straw”).

תורה.etymologyText: Representing a *tawrawat- prefixed from Proto-West Semitic *waraw- (“to throw, cast, lead, guide”).[1] Compare Aramaic אוֹרַיְתָא (ʾōrayṯā), Ge'ez ኦሪት (ʾorit).

תחש.etymologyText: Compare Arabic دُخَس (duḵas). In the “badger” sense, a phono-semantic matching of German Dachs.

תיש.etymologyText: Compare Aramaic תֵּישָׁא / תַּיְשָׁא (tēšā / tayšā), Arabic تَيْس (tays).

תמה.etymologyText: Related to Arabic تَمِهَ (tamiha), Aramaic תְּמַהּ (təmah).

תמוז.etymologyText: From Akkadian 𒌗𒋗 (itiDuʾzu/Dūzu), from Sumerian 𒌉𒍣 (DUMU.ZID, “the true son”).

תמיד.etymologyText: Ernest Klein connects the term to Hebrew מוד, which is associated with מדד (“to measure”) and the Arabic مَدَّ (madda, “to stretch, prolong”). He also notes that Hommel links it to Arabic تَأْمِيد (taʔmīd, “fixing, establishing”), the verbal noun of أَمَّدَ (ʔammada). Furthermore, Klein reports that Geiger and Peres consider it a contraction of תעמיד, derived from עמד (“to stand”). Conversely, Even-Shoshan identifies מוד as the root and Arabic مَادَ (māda) as a cognate, while also mentioning tha

תנור.etymologyText: Loanword from Akkadian 𒅎𒋗𒆸 (tinūrum). Compare also Middle Persian tnwl (tanūr, “oven”). This word has been borrowed into Aramaic as תנורא / ܬܰܢܽܘܪܳܐ (tannūrā) and therethrough spawned Arabic تَنُّور (tannūr).

תנין.etymologyText: From Akkadian 𒆗𒉌𒉡 (danninu, “netherworld; source of earthquakes; the inaccessible land where the dead remain”), whence also Aramaic תַּנִּינָא / ܬܱܢܺܝܢܳܐ (tannīnā, “sea serpent, monster”) and Ugaritic 𐎚𐎐𐎐 (tnn).

תקן.etymologyText: Compare with Arabic تِقن (tiqn, “improvement, perfection”) and تَقَانَة (taqāna, “firmness, solidity”)

תרגם.etymologyText: Compare Aramaic תרגם, Arabic تَرْجَمَ (tarjama), Ge'ez ተርጐመ (tärgʷämä).

תשעים.etymologyText: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *tišʿū-. Cognate with Arabic تِسْعُونَ (tisʕūna).

אביב.etymologyText: From the root meaning "to be thick," "to swell," or "to ripen." Possible cognate to Arabic أَبّ (ʔabb, “pasture, herbage”). Not related to Coptic ⲉⲡⲏⲡ (epēp, “November”), a false friend.

אביון.etymologyText: Cognate with Ugaritic 𐎀𐎁𐎊𐎐 (ảbyn, “poor, impoverished”). Borrowed into Late Egyptian, producing Coptic ⲉⲃⲓⲏⲛ (ebiēn, “miserable, wretched”).

אהבה.etymologyText: Properly the infinitive construct of אָהַב (aháv, “to love”).[1] Compare Ugaritic 𐎀𐎅𐎁𐎚 (ảhbt).

אות.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *awayat-, cognate with Aramaic אתא (ʾāṯāh, “sign”) and Arabic آية (ʔāya, “sign”).

אחי.etymologyText: From אח (akh, “brother of”) +‎ ־י (-í, “my”). Cognate with Arabic أَخِ (akh)

אלון.etymologyText: Uncertain; doublet of אֵלוֹן (elón), which possibly is the native Canaanite counterpart, compare Aramaic אִילָנָא (ʾīlānā, “tree”) and Classical Syriac ܐܺܝܠܳܢܳܐ (ʾīlānā, “tree”). The present form with a short /a/ and a geminated /l/ on the other hand may be a borrowing from Akkadian 𒀠𒆷𒀭 (ʾallānu, alyānu, “oak; acorn”). For a similar situation see אֵלָה (elá) and אַלָּה (alá).

אילן.etymologyText: Borrowed from Aramaic אִילָנָא / ܐܺܝܠܳܢܳܐ (ʾīlānā, “tree”). Doublet of אֵלוֹן (elōn, “great tree”) and אַלּוֹן (allōn, “great tree; oak”).

אכלה.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔuklat-. Feminine of אוכל / אֹכֶל (“food”), or a feminine infinitive form of the verb אָכַל (“to eat”). Compare Arabic أُكْلَة (ʔukla).

אלוף.etymologyText: From root א־ל־ף (“to associate”). Cognate with Arabic أَلُوف (ʔalūf).

אסר.etymologyText: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔasar-; cognate with Arabic أَسَرَ (ʔasara, “to capture, seize”), etc.

אפרים.etymologyText: According to the Book of Genesis, from a word meaning "being fruitful;" compare Aramaic 𐡐𐡀𐡓𐡀 (pera, “fruit”).[1]

אשה.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ʔanθ-at-. Cognate with Ugaritic 𐎀𐎘𐎚 (ảṯt), Aramaic אִנְתְּתָא (ʾintəṯā), אִיתְּתָא (ʾittəṯā), Arabic أُنْثَى (ʔunṯā).

בית.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *bayt- (“house”). Cognate with Akkadian 𒂍 (bītum), Arabic بَيْت (bayt) and Amharic ቤት (bet).

ברד.etymologyText: Compare Aramaic בַּרְדָא (barḏā), Arabic بَرَد (barad), Ge'ez በረድ (bäräd).

גלות.etymologyText: From גָּלָה (galá, “to be exiled”) +‎ ־וּת (-út). Compare Aramaic גָּלוּתָא (gālūṯā), Classical Syriac ܓܠܘܬܐ (gālūṯā) Arabic جلاء (jalā').

גשם.etymologyText: Compare Ugaritic 𐎂𐎌𐎎 (gšm, “rain, downpour”). The sense "body" (and, by extension, "substance") is first attested in Aramaic parts of the Book of Daniel and later gained currency in Medieval Hebrew. This sense appears to represent a borrowing from Aramaic, for which compare Classical Syriac ܓܘܫܡܐ and confer Arabic جِسْم (jism).

דבק.etymologyText: Compare Arabic دِبْق (dibq, “birdlime”) and دَبِقَ (dabiqa, “to stick, adhere, cleave, cling”); also Classical Syriac ܕܘܒܩܐ (dubbāqā, “birdlime”) (from ܕܒܩ (dbaq, “to stick”)).

דוב.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *dubb- (“bear”). Cognate with Arabic دُبٌّ (dubbun, “bear”). Named after either their slow and soft gait,[1][2] or their murmuring.[3]

דין.etymologyText: Cognate with Arabic دِين (dīn), Aramaic דִּינָא (dīnā), Amharic ዳኛ (daña) and Ugaritic 𐎄𐎊𐎐 (dyn).

דלי.etymologyText: Either derived or merely related to דָּלָה (dalá, “to dangle, suspend”), as buckets were hanging above the water in a well. Compare Classical Syriac ܕܰܘܠܳܐ (dawlā), Arabic دَلْو (dalw), as well as Old Armenian դոյլ (doyl), a Semitic borrowing.

דרור.etymologyText: Borrowed from Akkadian 𒀭𒁺𒊏𒊒 (andurāru, “remission of debts, manumission of slaves, cancelling of illegal impositions on free persons”) or 𒁕𒊏𒊒 (darāru, “freedom; to become free of a task, to move about freely, to run off”).

זכוכית.etymologyText: Compare Aramaic זְכוּכִיתָא (zkūkītā), זְגוּגִיתָא (zgūgītā), Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܙܓ݂ܘܿܓ݂ܝܼܬ݂ܵܐ (zḡōḡīṯā), Akkadian 𒍝𒅗𒅗𒌈 (/⁠zakakatu⁠/) and Arabic زُجَاج (zujāj).

זן.etymologyText: Via Aramaic זנא / זנה / ܙܢܐ descending from Proto-Iranian *jánHah, Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́ánHas.

זנב.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ḏanab-. Cognate with Arabic ذَنَب (tail, end).

זרוע.etymologyText: From Proto-Semitic *ḏirāʕ- (“arm”). Compare Aramaic דְּרָעָא (dərāʿā), Arabic ذِرَاع (ḏirāʕ).

חבקוק.etymologyText: Uncertain; possibly comes from חָבַק (ḥāḇaq, “embrace”), from the root ח־ב־ק (“embrace”) or perhaps from Akkadian 𒄩𒄠𒁀𒄣𒄣 (ḫambaqūqu [ḫa-am-ba-qu-qu], “garden herb”).

חד.etymologyText: From Aramaic חד, which is cognate with Hebrew אֶחָד (ekhád, “one”).
